```{r setup}
library(totalevalerror)
```

This vignette replicates the spirit of Appendix D.7 (variance underestimation simulation) from Messing (2026) at a small-N scale. The full `n_sim = 1000` study lives in `analysis/04g2_sim_underestimation_balanced.R` of the paper repo.

## A small Monte Carlo

```{r small_mc, eval = FALSE}
# This block is set to eval = FALSE because n_sim = 50 is still ~30s on a
# laptop. Remove `eval = FALSE` to run.
scenarios <- tibble::tibble(
  N = c(30L, 60L),
  V = 3L, M = 2L, H = 1L, R = 2L,
  variances = list(
    list(item = 0.20, prompt = 0.05, item_x_prompt = 0.04,
         item_x_judge = 0.10, cell_level = 0.02, replicate = 0.15),
    list(item = 0.20, prompt = 0.05, item_x_prompt = 0.04,
         item_x_judge = 0.10, cell_level = 0.02, replicate = 0.15)
  )
)
out <- tee_sim_coverage(scenarios, n_sim = 50, seed = 1)
out
```

## What to look for

`tee_sim_coverage()` returns one row per (scenario, component) with:
- `truth`: the planted variance.
- `mean_est`: average REML estimate across simulations.
- `bias`: `mean_est - truth`. Should be near zero at moderate `N`.
- `rmse`: root mean squared error.

Bias should approach zero as `N` grows; RMSE should shrink with `sqrt(N)`. The full Appendix D.7 study uses `n_sim = 1000` and finds bias <2% on every component at `N >= 50`.
